content: Dorothy Bird Nyswander (1894–1988) was an American health educator who earned her doctorate in psychology from the University of California, Berkeley. She is widely regarded as the Mother of Health Education. Her professional career spanned over six decades and extended across multiple continents. During this time, Nyswander was a staunch advocate for community health and human rights. As a single mother, she balanced teaching high school with earning her doctorate. During the Great Depression, she worked for the Works Progress Administration and later advocated for childcare support for working mothers while employed with the Federal Works Agency. She also promoted preventive school health as the director of the Queen’s City Health Center. In 1943, Nyswander played a pivotal role in establishing the Berkeley School of Public Health. By 1946, she became a full-time professor at UC Berkeley, where she remained for nearly 12 years. After retiring in 1957 at the age of 62, she embarked on a 16-year career with the World Health Organization, traveling to countries such as Jamaica, Turkey, Brazil, the South Seas, and India to develop health education programs. Although she expressed regret about not entering politics, she acknowledged, You don’t get to do everything you want in this life. In 1966, Nyswander defined an open society as one where justice is equal for all, dissent is taken seriously as a sign of something wrong or needed, diversity is expected, the best healthcare is accessible to everyone, poverty is seen as a community disgrace rather than an individual failing, and the desire for power is replaced by the satisfaction of using power for the benefit of others. In 1996, two years before her death, the California Chapter of the Society for Public Health Education (NC-SOPHE) established the Dorothy B. Nyswander Award for Leadership in Health Education. This award honors health educators who exemplify the professional standards set by Nyswander. The first recipient was Helen Ross, former Chair of the San José State University MPH Program. Other recipients have included Kathleen Roe, former MPH Program Director and Chair of the SJSU Health Science Department; Meredith Minkler, Professor of Health and Social Behavior at UC Berkeley; and Kate Lorig, Professor in the Stanford University Department of Medicine and Director of the Patient Education Research Center. In 2005, the national Society for Public Health Education created the Open Society Award to honor Nyswander’s legacy. This award is presented annually to an individual or group that embodies and promotes the principles of an open society through research, practice, or teaching. The first recipient of this award was the San José State University Department of Health Science Master of Public Health Program.
